We say that the equation is \emph{non-trivially partition regular} if every finite colouring of $S$ has a monochromatic solution in which each variable is distinct.

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on the number of colours $r$ to show that there exists $N_r \in {\mathbb N}$ such that however $[N_r]$ is $r$-coloured there exist $x_1, x_2, x_3 \in [N_r]$ all of the same colour with $x_1+x_2 = x_3$.

The base case of 1-colourings follows on taking $N_1 = 2$, so we may assume that $r \geqslant 2$.  Let $N$ be a large positive integer, whose size (depending on $r$) is to be determined, and fix an $r$-colouring
$$
[N] = C_1 \cup \dots \cup C_r.
$$
Set $M := N_{r-1}$ and consider two possibilities.

\noindent\textbf{The inhomogeneous case: Some colour class $C_i$ is not $M$-homogeneous in $[N]$.}  From the definition of homogeneity it follows that there exists a positive integer $q$ such that $q\cdot [M]\subset [N]$ and $q \cdot [M] \cap C_i = \emptyset$.  On setting $C_j' := \left\{x \in [M] : qx \in C_j\right\}$ we induce an $(r-1)$-colouring
$$
[M] = \bigcup_{j \neq i} C_j'.
$$
Since $M = N_{r-1}$ it follows from our induction hypothesis that there exist $x_1', x_2', x_3' \in C_j'$ such that $x_1' + x_2' = x_3'$.  Schur's theorem follows in this case on setting $x_t := qx_t'$ for $t =1, 2, 3$.

\noindent\textbf{The homogeneous case: All colour classes are $M$-homogeneous in $[N]$.}  In this case it turns out that every colour class contains a solution to the Schur equation, provided that $N$ is sufficiently large in terms of $r$.  To prove this we invoke the following.\begin{claim}
For any $\delta > 0$ and $M \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $N_0 = N_0(\delta, M)$ such that for any $N \geqslant N_0$ if $A \subset [N]$ has $|A| \geqslant \delta N$ and $B\subset [N]$ is $M$-homogeneous in $[N]$ then there exist $x, x' \in A$ and $y \in B$ such that $x - x' = y$.
\end{claim}
The claim settles the homogeneous case of Schur's theorem on taking $A =B$ to be any colour class, since $M$-homogeneous sets have density at least $M^{-2} + o(1)$ in $[N]$ (see Lemma \ref{homogeneous density lemma};  one could have alternatively taken the largest colour class).  

To prove the claim we invoke Szemer\'edi's theorem!\footnote{The claim itself is not deep, for instance it is readily obtained from \cite[Theorem 4]{CRS07}. Our proof is designed to set the stage for the general setting of Part \ref{higher part}, when we will invoke the multidimensional polynomial Szemer\'edi theorem of Bergelson and Leibman \cite{BergelsonLeibman}.} This yields $N_0 = N_0(\delta, M)$ such that for any $N \geqslant N_0$ if $A \subset [N]$ with $|A| \geqslant \delta N$ then $A$ contains an arithmetic progression of length $M+1$, so that there exist $x$ and $q > 0$ for which
$$
x,\quad x+q,\quad x + 2q, \quad \dots,\quad x + Mq\quad \in  A.
$$
Notice that $q \cdot [M]  \subset [N]$, so $M$-homogeneity of $B$ implies that there exists $y \in q\cdot [M] \cap B$.  Taking $x' = x + y$ establishes the claim and completes our proof of Schur's theorem.

label: homogeneous density lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{homogeneous density lemma}
If $B \subset [N]$ is $M$-homogeneous in $[N]$ then
                                            
$$
|B| \geqslant \frac{1}{M}\left\lfloor \frac{N}{M} \right\rfloor.
$$
head: environment
name: Homogeneous sets are dense

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by a variant of Varnavides averaging \cite{varnavides}.  For each $q \leqslant N/M$ the definition of homogeneity gives
$$
B \cap  q \cdot [M] \neq \emptyset.
$$
Summing over $q$ then yields
$$
\sum_{q \leqslant N/M} |B\cap q \cdot [M]| \geqslant \left\lfloor N/M \right\rfloor.
$$
Interchanging the order of summation, we see that
\begin{align*}
\sum_{x \in B} \#\left\{(q, m) \in [N/M]\times [M] : x = qm\right\} \geqslant \left\lfloor N/M \right\rfloor.
\end{align*}
The result follows on noting that 
$$
\#\left\{(q, m) \in [N/M]\times [M] : x = qm\right\} \leqslant M.
$$

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us assume that $A \subset [N]^d$ has size at least $\delta N^d$ and lacks solutions to \eqref{multidim sarkozy eqn} with $y_i \in B_i$, where the $B_i$ are $M$-homogeneous sets. Setting $A_0 := A$, we iteratively apply Lemma \ref{density increment lemma} to obtain a sequence of sets $A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots$, each contained in an ambient grid $[N_n]^d$ with 
$$
N_n \geqslant N^{c^n}, \qquad |A_n| \geqslant \left( \delta + nc_d(\delta M^{-d})^6 \right) N_n^d.
$$
If this iteration continues until $n$ is sufficiently large in terms of $d,\delta, M$, we obtain a density exceeding 1, which would be impossible.  Hence for some $n \ll_{d, \delta, M} 1$ the inequality \eqref{increment inequality} is satisfied with $N_n$ in place of $N$ therein.  Therefore
$$
N \leqslant N_n^{C^n}\leqslant \left( C_d(\delta^{-1} M^d)^{C} \right)^{C^n} \ll_{ d, \delta, M} 1.
$$

head: environment
name: Generalised von Neumann theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the result for $i = 1$, the other case being similar. For ${\alpha} = ({\alpha}_1, \ldots, {\alpha}_d) \in {\mathbb T}^d$, define 
$$
S_B(\alpha) := \sum_{y \in B\cap [\sqrt{N}]^d} e(\alpha_1 y_1^2 + \dots + \alpha_d y_d^2).
$$
By orthogonality and H\"older's inequality, we have
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
|T_B(f_1, f_2)| &= \left|  \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} S_B(\alpha)\hat{f}_1(-\alpha) \hat{f}_2(\alpha) \mathrm{d}\alpha\right|\\
& \leqslant \left\| S_B\right\|_{L^6(\mathbb{T}^d)} \big\| \hat{f}_1 \big\|^{1/3}_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}\big\| \hat{f}_1 \big\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)}^{2/3} \big\| \hat{f}_2 \big\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
The result now follows on incorporating Parseval's identity 
\[
\big\| \hat{f}_i \big\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)} = \big\| f_i \big\|_{L^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)} \leqslant N^{d/2}
\]
together with the estimate
$$
\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} |S_B(\alpha)|^6 \mathrm{d}\alpha \ll_d N^{2d}.
$$
The latter mean value estimate follows from orthogonality and Theorem \ref{unrestricted lower bound}.

label: popularity lower bound
title: Proof
body_md:
For $q, n \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ write $q^{\otimes 2} \otimes n$ for the tuple $(q_1^2 n_1, \dots, q_d^2n_d)$ and write $q^{\otimes2} \otimes [N]^d$ for the set
$$
 \left\{q^{\otimes 2} \otimes n : n \in [N]^d\right\}.
$$
Let $N_0 = N_0(\delta/2^{1+d}, d, M)$ be the quantity given by Theorem \ref{multidimensional sarkozy}.  Suppose that $N \geqslant N_0$ and write $Q := \left\lfloor \sqrt{N/N_0} \right\rfloor$. Averaging, we have
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \sum_{q\in [Q]^d} |A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes2} \otimes [N_0]^d \right)|  \geqslant \delta (NQN_0)^d.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $Q$, there are at most $(2N)^d$ choices for $z$ for which there exists $q \in [Q]^d$ such that
$$
|A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes2} \otimes [N_0]^d \right)| \neq 0.
$$
Hence there are at least $\tfrac{1}{2} \delta (NQ)^{d}$ choices for $(z, q) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times \mathbb{N}^d$ for which 
\begin{equation}\label{popularity lower bound}
\begin{split}
|A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes2} \otimes [N_0]^d \right)| \geqslant 2^{-1-d}\delta N_0^d.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Call each such choice of $(z, q)$ a \emph{good} tuple.  Define
$$
A_{z, q} := \left\{ y \in [N_0]^d : z + q^{\otimes 2} \otimes y \in A\right\}.
$$
If $(z,q)$ is good then $|A_{z, q}| \geqslant 2^{-1-d} \delta N_0^d$.  Applying Theorem \ref{multidimensional sarkozy} we see that there exist $x, x' \in A_{z, q}$ satisfying \eqref{2nd multidim eqn} with the $y_i$ restricted to the $M$-homogeneous sets
$$
\left\{y_i : q_i y_i \in B_i\right\}.
$$
Translating and dilating, we deduce that each set $A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes2} \otimes [N_0]^d \right))$ satisfying \eqref{popularity lower bound} contains a solution to \eqref{2nd multidim eqn} with $y_i \in B_i$.  


For fixed $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times \mathbb{N}^d$ define $R(x,y)$ to be the quantity
$$
\#\left\{(z,q) \in \mathbb{Z}^{d}\times [Q]^d : \left\{x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2}\right\}  \subset \left( z + q^{\otimes 2} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)\right\}.
$$
\begin{claim}
$R(x,y) \leqslant N_0^{2d}.$
\end{claim}
\noindent To see this, observe that if $\left\{x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2}\right\} \subset z + q^{\otimes 2} \otimes [N_0]^{d} $ then for each $i$ there exists $m_i \in [N_0]$ such that 
$
y_i^{2} =  q_i^2 m_i.
$
As there are at most $N_0$ choices for $m_i$ for fixed $y_i$, there are at most $N_0^d$ choices for $q$.
Once one has fixed this choice of $q$ we have
$$
z \in x - q^{\otimes 2} \otimes [N_0]^d,
$$
so there are at most $N_0^d$ choices of $z$ for fixed $x$.  This establishes the claim.

Invoking the claim gives
\begin{multline*}
              
  N_0^{2d} \#\left\{(x, y) \in\mathbb{Z}^{d} \times B_1\times \dotsm \times B_d : \left\{x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2}\right\}  \subset A\right\} \\                                                                                                                                                                           
 \geqslant  \sum_{\substack{x \in \mathbb{Z}^n, y \in B_1\times \dotsm B_d\\ x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2} \in A}} R(x,y).
             
\end{multline*}
Next we interchange the order of summation to find that
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\substack{x \in \mathbb{Z}^d, y \in B_1\times \dotsm B_d\\ x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2} \in A}} & R(x,y)\\ & \geqslant \sum_{z\in \mathbb{Z}^d} \sum_{q \in [Q]^d} \#\left\{(x,y) : \left\{x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2}\right\} \subset A \cap \left(  z + q^{\otimes 2}\otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)\right\}\\
&  \geqslant \#\left\{(z,q)\in \mathbb{Z}^{d} \times [Q]^d: (z,q) \text{ is good}\right\} \\
&  \geqslant \tfrac{1}{2} \delta (NQ)^{d}.
\end{align*}
It follows that
\begin{multline*}
\#\left\{(x, y) \in\mathbb{Z}^{d} \times B_1\times \dotsm \times B_d : \left\{x,\ x+y^{\otimes 2}\right\}  \subset A\right\} \\
\geqslant \tfrac{1}{2} \delta N_0^{-2d} N^d \left\lfloor \sqrt{N/N_0} \right\rfloor^d.
\end{multline*}
The result follows since $N_0 \ll_{\delta, d, M} 1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove a more general result for sums of $d$ squares.  First note that, by translation, Proposition \ref{varnavides} remains valid for dense subsets of $[-N, N]^d$.
Given $A \subset [N]$ of density at least $\delta$, define
$$
A' := \left\{ x \in [-N, N]^d : x_1 + \dots + x_d \in A\right\}
$$
For every element $n$ of $[-N, N]$ there are at least $N$ pairs $(n_1, n_2) \in [-N, N]^2$ such that $n = n_1 + n_2$.  An induction then shows that for each $n \in [-N, N]$ we have
$$
\#\left\{(n_1, \dots, n_d) \in [-N, N]^d : n = n_1 + \dots + n_d\right\} \geqslant N^{d-1}.
$$
Consequently
$$
|A'| \geqslant \delta N^d \gg_d \delta |[-N, N]^d|.
$$
Applying Proposition \ref{varnavides} with $B_i := B$ for all $i$, we deduce that there are at least $c_0 N^{3d/2}$ tuples $(x, y) \in A' \times B^d$ such that $x + (y_1^2, \dots, y_d^2) \in A'$.
For each such tuple the sum $x = x_1 + \dots +x_d$ is an element of the one-dimensional set $A$, as is $x + y_1^2 + \dots + y_d^2$.  As each element of $A$ has at most $(2N+1)^{d-1}$ representations of the form $x_1 + \dots + x_d$, it follows that the number of solutions to 
                                
$$
x - x' = y_1^2 + \dots + y_d^2
$$
is at least
$$
c_0 N^{\frac{3d}2 - (d-1)} = c_0 N^{1 + \frac{d}{2}},
$$
as required.

\label{smooth varnavides}
Let $k_1, \dots, k_d, M \in \mathbb{N}$, $\eta, \delta \in (0,1]$, and  let $F \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ be  a finite set.   There exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $c_0 > 0$ such that for any $N \geqslant N_0$, if $A \subset [N]^d$ has $|A| \geqslant \delta N^d$ and $B\subset \mathbb{N} $ is $M$-homogeneous in the $N^\eta$-smooths, then the number of tuples $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times B^d$ for which \eqref{smooth poly config} holds is at least
$$
c_0 N^{d + \frac{1}{k_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{k_d}}.
$$

label: N eta large
title: Proof
body_md:
Increasing the size of $F$ if necessary, we may assume that $F$ contains two elements which differ in the $i$th coordinate for each $i \in [d]$.  Let $N_0$ be the quantity given by Corollary \ref{smooth multidimensional sarkozy generalisation} with respect to the density $\delta/ 2^{d+1}$.  Suppose that
\begin{equation}\label{N eta large}
N \geqslant  N_0^{1/\eta},
\end{equation}
and define the following sets of smooths:
$$
S_i := S\bigl( \bigl\lfloor \sqrt[k_i]{N/N_0} \bigr\rfloor; N^\eta \bigr).
$$  

Interchanging the order of summation, we have
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^{d}} \sum_{q_1\in S_1}\dots \sum_{q_d \in S_d} |A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)|  \geqslant \delta |S_1|\dotsm |S_d|(NN_0)^{d}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
Notice that there are at most $(2N)^{d}$ choices for $z$ for which there exists $q \in S_1\times \dots \times S_d$ such that
$$
|A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)| \neq 0.
$$
Hence  there are at least $\tfrac{1}{2} \delta N^{d}|S_1|\dotsm |S_d|$ choices for $(z,q) \in \mathbb{Z}^{d}\times \prod_i S_i$ for which 
\begin{equation}\label{smooth popularity lower bound}
\begin{split}
|A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)| \geqslant 2^{-d-1}\delta N_0^{d}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Call such a choice of $(z,q)$ a \emph{good} tuple.\\[5pt] \noindent
\textbf{Claim 1.}  For each good tuple $(z,q)$ the set $A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)$ contains a configuration of the form $x+y^{\otimes k}\otimes F$ for some $x \in {\mathbb Z}^d$ and some $y \in B^d$.        
                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
                

To see this, define
$$
A_{z, q} := \left\{ x \in [N_0]^{d} : z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes x  \in A\right\}.
$$
Then $|A_{z, q}| \geqslant 2^{-d-1} \delta N_0^{d}$.  Let 
$$
B_i = \left\{y_i \in [N_0]: q_i y_i \in B\right\} \cup (N_0, \infty).
$$ 
Using the fact that $B$ is $N^\eta$-smoothly $M$-homogeneous, together with \eqref{N eta large}, one can check that each $B_i$ is $M$-homogeneous (not just smoothly homogeneous).  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
Invoking Corollary \ref{smooth multidimensional sarkozy generalisation}, we see that there exist $x \in \mathbb{Z}^{d}$ and $y \in B_1\times \dots \times B_d$ such that 
$$
x + y^{\otimes k} \otimes F \subset A_{z,q}.
$$
Translating and dilating, we deduce that $A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)$ contains a configuration of the form $x'+(q\otimes y)^{\otimes k}\otimes F$.  By definition of the $B_i$ and the fact that $F$ is non-constant in each coordinate, we see that $y\in [N_0]^d$ and thus each coordinate of $q\otimes y$ lies in $B$.  This establishes Claim 1.    

For fixed $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times \mathbb{N}^d$ let $G(x,y)$ denote the number of  tuples $(z,q) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times \mathbb{N}^d$ satisfying 
\begin{equation}\label{xy config}
x + y^{\otimes k} \otimes F \subset z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d}.
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{A} := \left\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times B^d : x+y^{\otimes k} \otimes F \subset A\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then interchanging the order of summation shows that the sum $\sum_{(x,y) \in \mathcal{A}}G(x,y)$ is at least
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^{d}} \sum_{q_1\in S_1}\dots \sum_{q_d \in S_d} \Bigl|\left\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times B^d : x+y^{\otimes k}\otimes F \subset A \cap \left( z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} \right)\right\} \Bigr|\\
& \geqslant \Bigl|  \Bigl\{ (z, q) \in \mathbb{Z}^d \times \prod_i S_i : (z,q) \text{ is good} \Bigr\} \Bigr| \geqslant \tfrac{1}{2} \delta N^{d}|S_1|\dotsm |S_d|.
\end{align*}
Applying Lemma \ref{dense smooths} (for $N$ sufficiently large) we deduce that
$$
\sum_{(x,y) \in \mathcal{A}}G(x,y) \gg_{k, \delta, \eta, N_0}\ N^{d + \frac{1}{k_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{k_d}}.
$$  
Since the theorem asserts a lower bound on the size of $\mathcal{A}$, the result is proved provided we have the following upper bound on $G(x,y)$.\\[5pt]\noindent
\textbf{Claim 2.} Suppose that $F$ contains two elements which differ in the $i$th coordinate for each $i \in [d]$.  Then $G(x,y) \leqslant N_0^{2d}$.\\[5pt]\noindent

To see this, first note that if $x+y^{\otimes k}\otimes F \subset z + q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^{d} $ then, since $F$ contains two elements differing in their $i$th coordinate, there exist integers $f_i < f_i'$ such that 
$$
x_i + y_i^{k_i} f_i, \ x_i + y_i^{k_i} f_i' \in z_i + q_i^{k_i} \cdot [N_0].
$$
Subtracting these elements, we deduce that there exists $n_i \in [N_0]$ for which
$$
 q_i^{k_i} = \frac{y_i^{k_i} (f_i'- f_i)}{n_i}.
$$
As there are at most $N_0$ choices for $n_i$, and $y_i$ is fixed, there are at most $N_0^d$ choices for $q$.
Once one has fixed this choice of $q$, for any $f \in F$ we have
$$
z \in x + y^{\otimes k} \otimes f - q^{\otimes k} \otimes [N_0]^d,
$$
so there are at most $N_0^d$ choices for $z$.  In summary $G(x,y) \leqslant N_0^{2d}$, which establishes Claim 2.

title: Proof
body_md:
Given $A \subset [N]$ of density at least $\delta$, let us define
$$
\tilde{A} := \Bigl\{  x \in [N]^{s + t-2} : \sum_i x_i \in A \Bigr\}
$$
A stars and bars argument shows that for $n \in [N]$ we have
$$
\#\left\{(n_1, \dots, n_d) \in [N]^d : n = n_1 + \dots + n_d\right\} = \binom{n-1}{d-1}.
$$
Since there are at most $\tfrac{1}{2}|A|$ elements $x$ of $A$ satisfying the inequality $x \leqslant \tfrac{1}{2}|A|$, it follows that for $N \geqslant C_{s,t} \delta^{-1}$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{A tilde density}
|\tilde{A}| = \sum_{n \in A} \binom{n-1}{s+t-3} \gg_{s,t} \delta^{s+t-2} N^{s+t-2}.
\end{equation}

In the statement of Theorem \ref{smooth super saturated sarkozy generalisation}, at least one of the coefficients $\lambda_i$ must be positive.  Relabelling indices, we may assume that $\lambda_{s} > 0$. For a technical reason, it will be useful in a later part of the argument if we can ensure that 
  \begin{equation}\label{width assumption}
  \tilde{A} - \tilde{A} \subset \left[ -\tfrac{N}{\lambda_s},\tfrac{N}{\lambda_s} \right]^{s+t-2}.
  \end{equation}
This follows on partitioning the hypercube $[N]^{s+t-2}$ into subhypercubes of sufficiently small side length and applying the pigeonhole principle to ensure that $\tilde{A}$ has large density on one such part (worsening the density \eqref{A tilde density} by a factor of $O_{s,t, \lambda_s}(1)$ in the process).
  
Define $F \subset \mathbb{Z}^{s+t-2}$ to be the set consisting of the zero vector together with the rows         
 of the following matrix
 \begin{equation}\label{F matrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}
                               
-\lambda_s & \ & \ &\ & \ & \ & \ \\
\ & -\lambda_s & \ &\  & \ & \ & \ \\
 \ & \ & \ddots &\  & \  & \ & \ \\
  \ & \ & \ &- \lambda_{s} & \  & \ & \ \\
 \lambda_1 & \lambda_2 & \dots &\lambda_{s-2} & \lambda_s^{k-1} \mu_1 & \dots & \lambda_s^{k-1}\mu_t
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \end{equation}
    
                  
                                                                          
                                                                                     
                                                                         
                                                                                        
                                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                        
                
    
   
                                                                                                                                                               
    
Consider the set
  $$
 \tilde{B} := \left\{ y \in \mathbb{N} : \lambda_{s} y \in B\right\} \cup (N^{1/k}\lambda_s^{-1}, \infty) .
$$
Provided that $N^\eta \geqslant \max\left\{\lambda_s, M\right\}$ (as we may assume), we see that $\tilde{B}$ is $M$-homogeneous in the $N^\eta$-smooths.
Applying Theorem \ref{smooth varnavides}, we find that there are at least $c_0 N^{s+t-2 + s-2 +\frac{t}{k}}$
                             
 tuples $(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{s+t - 2} \times \tilde{B}^{s-2} \times \tilde{B}^t$ such that $\tilde{A}$ contains the configuration 
 $$
x + (y_1, \dots, y_{s-2}, z_1^k, \dots, z_t^k)\otimes F.
 $$  
By \eqref{width assumption} and \eqref{F matrix} we have $\lambda_s^k \mu_i z_i^k \in [-N, N]$, hence by definition of $\tilde{B}$ we deduce that $\lambda_s z_i \in B$.
 Projecting down to one dimension and taking into account the multiplicities of representations, we obtain $\gg N^{s +\frac{t}{k}- 1}$ tuples $(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}^{s-2} \times \mathbb{N}^t$ with $\lambda_sz_i \in B$ and such that $A$ contains the  configuration
 \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
x,\quad x-\lambda_sy_1 ,\quad \dots,\quad x-\lambda_s y_{s-2},\quad 
 x + \sum_{i=1}^{s-2}\lambda_iy_i +\lambda_s^{k-1}\sum_{j=1}^t \mu_jz_j^k.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
Let us set  $x_i := x -\lambda_s y_i$ for $i=1, \dots, s-2$, along with $x_{s-1} = x$ and
$$
x_{s} :=x + \sum_{i=1}^{s-2}\lambda_iy_i +\lambda_s^{k-1}\sum_{j=1}^t \mu_jz_j^k.
$$ 
One can then check that the tuple $(x_1, \dots, x_s, \lambda_{s}z_1, \dots, \lambda_s z_t)$ is an element of $A^s \times B^t$ satisfying 
\eqref{smooth one dim equation}.  By construction there are $\gg N^{s +\frac{t}{k} - 1}$ such tuples.

body_md:
We employ \eqref{smooth A1 size} in conjunction with \eqref{number of smooths} to conclude that
\begin{align*}
&\# \Bigl\{  x \in S(P;P^\eta) :  x \equiv \xi \bmod W, \quad \frac{x^k - \xi^k}{kW} \in A_1, \quad x > Z \Bigr\} \\
& \geqslant |A_1| - ZW^{-1} - 1 \\
&  \geqslant  \tfrac{\delta }{2} \#\left\{x \in S(P; P^\eta) : x \equiv \xi \bmod W\right\} - ZW^{-1} - O_{\eta, \delta, w}\left(  N(\log N)^{-1} \right)  \\
& \geqslant \tfrac{\delta}{2W} |S(P; P^\eta)| -ZW^{-1} - O_{\eta, \delta, w}\left( N(\log N)^{-1} \right).
\end{align*}
Choosing
$$
Z = \frac \delta 4 |S(P;P^\eta)|
$$
furnishes
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n \in A_1} \nu(n) & \geqslant \tfrac{(\delta/4)^k}{W} |S(P; P^\eta)|^k - O_{\eta,\delta, w}\left( N
^k(\log N)^{-1} \right).
\end{align*}
Using Lemma \ref{dense smooths} and recalling \eqref{X and P} we obtain
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n \in A_1} \nu(n) & \geqslant W^{-1} ({\delta} P \rho(1/\eta)/4)^k  - O_{\eta,\delta, w}\left( N^k(\log N)^{-1} \right)
\\ & \geqslant (k (\rho(1/\eta)/4)^k) \cdot \delta^k X - O_{\eta,\delta, w}\left( N^k(\log N)^{-1} \right).
\end{align*}
Taking $N$ sufficiently large, an application of \eqref{smooth normalisation} completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
We employ Theorem \ref{smooth pseudorandom} with majorant $\nu$ given by \eqref{nu defn}, homogeneous set $B_1 \subset S(X^{1/k}; X^\eta)$ given by \eqref{B1 defn}, and function $f =  \nu 1_{A_1}$ (recall \eqref{A1 defn}). It is first necessary to check that these choices satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{smooth pseudorandom}.                                                                                                        

By Lemma \ref{smooth restriction}, the function $\nu$ satisfies a $(s+t-10^{-8})$-restriction estimate with constant $K = O_{\eta, k}(1)$.  Let $c_{\eta,k}$ denote the implied constant in \eqref{A1 density} and set $\tilde{\delta} := c_{\eta,k} \delta^k$.  Theorem \ref{smooth pseudorandom} guarantees the existence of a positive constant 
\begin{equation}\label{theta dependence}
\theta = \theta(\eta,\tilde\delta, M, K) 
\end{equation}
such that provided $\nu$ has Fourier decay of level $\theta$ and $\left\| f\right\|_1 \geqslant \tilde\delta \left\| \nu\right\|_1$ we may conclude that \eqref{smooth pseud conclusion} holds.  Taking 
$$
w = C_{\eta} \theta^k
$$
guarantees sufficient Fourier decay, by Lemma \ref{smooth decay}.  We note that this choice of $w$ satisfies $w \ll_{\eta,  \delta, M} 1$, as can be checked by unravelling the dependencies in \eqref{theta dependence}. We obtain $\left\| f\right\|_1 \geqslant \tilde\delta \left\| \nu\right\|_1$ via Lemma \ref{smooth density transfer}.  This requires us to take $N$  sufficiently large in terms of $k, \eta, w$ and $\delta$.  By our choice of $w$, this is ensured if $N$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\eta,  \delta$ and $M$ (as we may assume).

Applying Theorem \ref{smooth pseudorandom} and \eqref{smooth normalisation} yields
\[
T_1(\nu 1_{A_1}; B_1) \gg_{\eta, \delta, M} \|\nu\|_1^s X^{\frac t k -1}\gg_{\eta,\delta,M} X^{s+\frac t k -1}.
\]
By \eqref{smooth AA_1} and the bound $\|\nu\|_\infty \ll_{\eta,{\delta},M} N^{k-1}$, we finally have
\[
T_k(A;B) \geqslant T_1(A_1; B_1) \geqslant \| \nu \|_\infty^{-s} T_1(\nu 1_{A_1};  B_1) \gg_{\eta, {\delta},M} N^{s+t-k}.
\]

\label{modelling lemma}
Suppose that $\nu: [N] \to [0, \infty)$ satisfies a $p$-restriction estimate with constant $K$, and has Fourier decay of level $1/M$ with $M \geqslant M_0(p, K)$ .  Then for any $f_i : [N] \to [0, \infty)$ with $f_1 + \dots + f_r =  \nu$ there exists $g_i :  [N] \to [0, \infty)$ such that $ g_1 + \dots + g_r = (1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{M}})1_{[N]}$ and

$$

label: greedy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{greedy}
Let $W$ be a $w$-smooth positive integer divisible by the primorial $\prod_{p\leqslant w} p$.  For any sets $A \subset S \subset [N]$ with $|A| \geqslant \delta |S|$ and $|S| \geqslant  \eta N$, there exist a $w$-smooth number 
$
\zeta \ll_{{\delta}, \eta, w} 1,
$ 
and $\xi \in [W]$ with $(\xi,W) = 1$, such that  
$$
 \#\left\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : \zeta( \xi + W x ) \in A\right\} \geqslant \tfrac{1}{2}\delta\# \left\{x \in \mathbb{Z} :  \zeta( \xi + W x ) \in S\right\}.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\zeta, \xi \in {\mathbb N}$ and $T \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, write
$$
T_{\zeta, \xi, W} := \left\{x \in T : x= \zeta( \xi + W y ) \text{ for some } y \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}.
$$
Let $M = 4({\delta} \eta)^{-2} 10^{2w}$, so that $N10^w  M^{-1/2} = \frac {\delta} 2 \eta N \leqslant \frac {\delta} 2 |S|$. By the remarks preceding this lemma, together with Lemma \ref{rankin lemma}, we have
\begin{align*}
{\delta} |S| \leqslant |A| &\leqslant \sum_{\substack{\zeta \leqslant M\\ \zeta \text{ is $w$-smooth}}}\sum_{\substack{\xi \in [W] \\ \ (\xi, W) = 1}} |A_{\zeta, \xi, W}| + N10^w  M^{-1/2}
\\&
\leqslant  \sum_{\substack{\zeta \leqslant M\\ \zeta \text{ is $w$-smooth}}}\sum_{\substack{\xi \in [W] \\ \ (\xi, W) = 1}} |A_{\zeta, \xi, W}| + \frac {\delta} 2 |S|.
\end{align*}
Therefore
\[
\delta \sum_{\substack{\zeta \leqslant M\\ \zeta \text{ is $w$-smooth}}}\sum_{\substack{\xi \in [W] \\ \ (\xi, W) = 1}} |S_{\zeta, \xi, W}| \leqslant {\delta} |S| \leqslant 2\sum_{\substack{\zeta \leqslant M \\ \zeta \text{ is $w$-smooth}}}\sum_{\substack{\xi \in [W] \\ \ (\xi, W) = 1}} |A_{\zeta, \xi, W}|,
\]
and the pigeonhole principle completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:

\]

\[

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{unrestricted lower bound}
Let $c_1, \dots, c_s \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\left\{0\right\}$ with $\sum_{i \in I}c_i = 0$ for some non-empty subset $I$ of $[s]$. Then, for $k \geqslant 2$, there exists $s_0(k) \in {\mathbb N}$ such that if $s \geqslant s_0(k)$ and $N \geqslant N_0$ then
\[
\# \Bigl\{ {\mathbf x} \in S(N;N^\eta)^s : \sum_{i= 1}^s c_i x_i^k = 0 \Bigr\} \asymp_{{\mathbf{c}},\eta, k } N^{s-k}.
\]
Moreover, one can take $s_0(2) = 5$, $s_0(3) = 8$, and $s_0(k)$ satisfying \eqref{s0 size}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $k \geqslant 3$, and let $\eta = \eta_k$ be a small positive constant. By orthogonality, our count is
\[
\int_0^1 g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha},
\]
where 
\[
g({\alpha}) = \sum_{x \in S(N; N^\eta)} e({\alpha} x^k), \qquad g_i({\alpha}) = g(c_i {\alpha}) \quad (1 \leqslant i \leqslant s).
\]
Let $A \geqslant A_0(k)$, and put $Q = (\log N)^A$. Now perform a Hardy--Littlewood dissection \cite{vaughan97}: define major arcs
\[
{\mathfrak M} = \bigcup_{ \substack{ 0 \leqslant a < q \leqslant Q \\ (a,q) = 1} } {\mathfrak M}(q,a), 
\qquad {\mathfrak M}(q,a) = \{ {\alpha} \in [0,1]: | q {\alpha} - a| \leqslant QN^{-k} \}
\]
and minor arcs ${\mathfrak m} = [0,1] \setminus {\mathfrak M}$. It follows from \cite[Lemma 8.6]{DS2016}, by slightly adjusting the parameters therein to allow for constant multiples, that
\[
\int_{\mathfrak m} |g_i({\alpha})|^s {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} = c_i^{-1} \int_{c_i {\mathfrak m}} |g({\beta})|^s {\mathrm{d}} {\beta} \ll N^{s-k} Q^{-c},
\]
for some $c = c(k) > 0$. Therefore
\[
\int_0^1 g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} = \int_{\mathfrak M} g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} + o(N^{s-k}).
\]

First we prune our major arcs down to a lower height. Set $Q_1 = \sqrt{\log N}$. Let
\[
{\mathfrak N} = \bigcup_{\substack{0 \leqslant a < q \leqslant Q_1 \\ (a,q) = 1}} {\mathfrak N}(q,a), \qquad {\mathfrak N}(q,a) = \{ {\alpha} \in [0,1]: |q {\alpha} - a| \leqslant Q_1 N^{-k}  \},
\]
and put ${\mathfrak n} = [0,1] \setminus {\mathfrak N}$. Let ${\alpha} \in {\mathfrak M}(q,a)$ with $0 \leqslant a < q \leqslant Q$ and $(a,q) = 1$ and, by Dirichlet's approximation theorem \cite[Lemma 2.1]{vaughan97}, choose relatively prime $r \in {\mathbb N}$ and $b \in {\mathbb Z}$ such that $r \leqslant 2Q$ and $|r c_s {\alpha} - b| \leqslant (2Q)^{-1}$. The triangle inequality gives
\[
\Bigl| \frac a q - \frac b{rc_s} \Bigr| \leqslant \frac Q{qN^k} + \frac1 {2 rc_s Q} < \frac1{qrc_s},
\]
so $\frac a q = \frac b {rc_s}$. As $(a,q) = 1$ and $(rc_s, b) \ll 1$, we have $q \asymp r$, $|rc_s {\alpha} - b| \asymp |q {\alpha} - a|$, and it now follows from \cite[Lemma 8.5]{VW1991} that
\[
g_s({\alpha}) \ll_\varepsilon q^\varepsilon N (q + N^k | q {\alpha} - a| )^{-1/k} + N \exp(-c \sqrt{\log N}  ) (1 + N^k |{\alpha} - a/q|),
\]
where $c = c(A, \eta)$ is a small positive constant. In particular, if ${\alpha} \in {\mathfrak M} \setminus {\mathfrak N}$ then 
\[
g_s({\alpha}) \ll  N Q_1^{\varepsilon - 1/k}.
\]
Furthermore, the sharp mean value estimate \cite[Theorem 2.3]{DS2016} implies
\begin{equation} \label{dsmv}
\int_0^1 |g_i({\alpha})|^{s-0.1} {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} \ll N^{s-0.1-k} \qquad (1 \leqslant i \leqslant s).
\end{equation}
Using H\"older's inequality, we now obtain
\[
\int_{{\mathfrak M} \setminus {\mathfrak N}} |g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha})| {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} = o(N^{s-k}),
\]
and so
\begin{equation} \label{pruned}
\int_0^1 g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} = \int_{\mathfrak N} g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} + o(N^{s-k}).
\end{equation}

For $q \in {\mathbb N}$, $a \in {\mathbb Z}$ and ${\beta} \in {\mathbb R}$, define
\[
S(q,a) = \sum_{x \leqslant q} e_q(ax^k), \qquad w({\beta}) = \sum_{N^{\eta k} < m  \leqslant N^k} \frac 1k m^{\frac1k - 1} \rho\Bigl( \frac{\log m}{\eta k \log N} \Bigr) e({\beta} m)
\]
and
\[
W( {\alpha}, q, a) = q^{-1} S(q,a) w({\alpha} - a/q),
\]
where as before $\rho$ denotes the Dickman--de Bruijn $\rho$-function. Next, we apply \cite[Lemma 5.4]{Vau1989} to $c_i {\alpha}$, for $1 \leqslant i \leqslant s$ and ${\alpha} \in {\mathfrak N}(q,a) \subset {\mathfrak N}$, where $0 \leqslant a < q \leqslant Q_1$ and $|q {\alpha} - a| \leqslant Q_1 N^{-k}$. With $c'_i = c_i/(c_i,q)$ and $q_i = q/(c_i,q)$, this gives
\[
g_i({\alpha}) = W(c_i {\alpha}, q_i, c'_i a) + O( (\log N)^{-1/2}) ,
\]
and furthermore
\begin{equation} \label{MajorArcBound}
W(c_i {\alpha}, q, c_i a) = W(c_i {\alpha}, q_i, c_i' a) \ll q^{-1/k} \min(N, | {\alpha} - a/q |^{-1/k}).
\end{equation}
By \eqref{dsmv} and \eqref{pruned}, together with H\"older, we now have
\begin{align*}
&\int_0^1 g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} 
\\ & \quad =
\sum_{q \leqslant \sqrt{\log N}} q^{-s}  \sum_{\substack{a \leqslant q \\ (a,q)=1}} 
\int_{|{\beta}| \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\log N}} {q N^k}}
\Bigl(\prod_{i \leqslant s} S(q, c_i a) 
 w(c_i {\beta}) \Bigr) {\mathrm{d}} {\beta}
+ o(N^{s-k}).
\end{align*}

The bound \eqref{MajorArcBound} enables us to extend the integral to $[-1/2, 1/2]^s$ and then the outer sum to infinity with $o(N^{s-k})$ error, as is usual for a major arc analysis \cite{davenport, vaughan97}. We thus obtain
\[
\int_0^1 g_1({\alpha}) \cdots g_s({\alpha}) {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} = {\mathfrak S} J  + o(N^{s-k}),
\]
where 
\[
{\mathfrak S} = \sum_{q = 1}^\infty \sum_{\substack{a \leqslant q \\ (a,q) = 1}} q^{-s} S(q, c_1 a) \cdots S(q, c_s a)
\]
and
\[
J = \int_{[-1/2,1/2]^s} w(c_1 {\beta}) \cdots w(c_s {\beta}) {\mathrm{d}} {\beta}.
\]

As discussed in \cite[Ch. 8]{davenport}, the singular series is a product of $p$-adic densities,
\[
{\mathfrak S} = \prod_p \chi_p,
\]
and is strictly positive if and only if $\chi_p > 0$ for all $p$. The positivity of the $p$-adic densities $\chi_p$ follows from the assumption that $\sum_{i \in I} c_i = 0$ for some non-empty $I \subseteq [s]$: one takes a non-trivial solution in $\{ 0, 1 \}^s$, and this is a non-singular $p$-adic zero.

Our final task is to show that $J \asymp N^{s-k}$. By orthogonality
\[
J = k^{-s} \sum_{\substack{{\mathbf{m}} \in (N^{\eta k}, N^k]^s \\
{\mathbf{c}} \cdot {\mathbf{m}} = 0}} \prod_{i \leqslant s} m_i^{\frac1k -1} \rho \Bigl( \frac{ \log m_i } { \eta k \log N} \Bigr).
\]
With $c > 0$ small, we have the crude lower bound
\[
J \gg N^{s(1-k)} \sum_{ \substack{{\mathbf{m}} \in (cN^k, N^k]^s \\ {\mathbf{c}} \cdot {\mathbf{m}} = 0}} 1 \gg N^{s(1-k)} (N^k)^{s-1} = N^{s-k},
\]
since the $c_i$ are not all of the same sign. We also have the complementary upper bound
\[
J \ll N^{s(1-k)} \sum_{ \substack{{\mathbf{m}} \in [1, N^k]^s \\ {\mathbf{c}} \cdot {\mathbf{m}} = 0}} 1 \ll N^{s-k}.
\]

label: BabyRestriction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{BabyRestriction} Let
\[
f: [N] \to \{z \in {\mathbb C}: |z| \leqslant 1 \}.
\]
If $p > 4$ then
\[
\int_{\mathbb T} \Bigl|\sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta)} f(x) e({\alpha} x^2) \Bigr|^p {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} \ll _p N^{p-2}.
\]
For $k \geqslant 3$, there exists $s_0(k)$ such that if $s \geqslant s_0(k)$ then
\[
\int_{\mathbb T} \Bigl|\sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta)} f(x) e({\alpha} x^k) \Bigr|^{s - 10^{-8}} {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} \ll  N^{s - 10^{-8}-k}.
\]
Moreover, one may take $s_0(3) = 8$, and $s_0(k)$ satisfying \eqref{s0 size}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The quadratic statement is a direct consequence of \cite[Eq.\ (4.1)]{Bou1989}.                                                                                          
Assuming for the time being that $k \geqslant 4$, write $2t$ for the smallest even integer greater than or equal to the integer $s_0(k)$ appearing in Theorem \ref{unrestricted lower bound}. Note that modifying $s_0(k)$ by adding a constant does not affect the veracity of \eqref{s0 size}, and so we will prove the statement for $s\geqslant s_0(k)+2$ in this case. 

By orthogonality, the triangle inequality and Theorem \ref{unrestricted lower bound}, we have
\begin{align*}
&\int_{\mathbb T} \Bigl|\sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta)} f(x) e({\alpha} x^k) \Bigr|^{2t} {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} 
\\ &\qquad \leqslant
\# \Bigl\{ ({\mathbf x}, {\mathbf{y}}) \in S(N;N^\eta)^t \times S(N;N^\eta)^t : \sum_{i \leqslant t} x_i^k = \sum_{i \leqslant t} y_i^k \Bigr\} 
 \ll_{t, \eta} N^{ 2t - k}.
\end{align*}
The trivial estimate $\Bigl|\sum_{x \in S(N; N^\eta)} f(x) e({\alpha} x^k) \Bigr| \leqslant N$ completes the proof when $k \geqslant 4$.

For $k = 3$ we require a more elaborate argument to prove that the precise value of $s_0(3) = 8$ is admissible. In particular, our approach relies on a `subconvex' mean value estimate of Wooley \cite{Woo1995}. Define $\phi: {\mathbb Z} \to {\mathbb C}$ by $\phi(n) = f(x)$ if $n = x^3$ for some $x \in S(N; N^\eta)$, and zero otherwise. Our objective is to show that
\[
\int_{\mathbb T} | \hat \phi({\alpha})|^{8-10^{-8}} {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} \ll N^{5-10^{-8}}.
\]

In the present appendix, we let ${\delta}$ denote a parameter in the range
\[
0 < {\delta} < 1,
\]
and consider the large spectra
\[
\mathcal{R}_{\delta} = \{ {\alpha} \in {\mathbb T}: |\hat \phi({\alpha})| > {\delta} N \}.
\]
By the dyadic pigeonholing argument in \cite[\S 6]{densesquares}, it suffices to prove that
\[
\mathrm{meas}(\mathcal{R}_{\delta}) \ll \frac1{{\delta}^{8-10^{-7}}N^3}.
\]
By orthogonality, Wooley's estimate \cite[Theorem 1.2]{Woo1995} implies that
\[
\int_{\mathbb T} | \hat \phi({\alpha}) |^6 {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} \ll N^{3.25 - 10^{-4}}.
\]
Thus, we may assume without loss of generality that
\begin{equation} \label{wmaBounded}
N^{10^{-5} - \frac18} < {\delta} < 1.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if ${\delta} \leqslant N^{10^{-5} -\frac18}$ then 
\[
\mathrm{meas}(\mathcal{R}_{\delta})  \leqslant ({\delta} N)^{-6} \int_{\mathcal{R}_{\delta}} |\hat \phi({\alpha})|^6 {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha} \ll ({\delta} N)^{-6} N^{3.25-10^{-4}} \leqslant \frac1{{\delta}^{8-10^{-7}}N^3}.
\]

Let ${\theta}_1, {\theta}_2, \ldots, {\theta}_R$ be $N^{-3}$-separated points in $\mathcal{R}_{\delta}$. As $8-10^{-7}\geqslant 6.3$ it suffices to show that
\begin{equation} \label{STPcubicBounded}
R \ll {\delta}^{-6.3}.
\end{equation}
Let $\mu(n) = 1$ if $n = x^3$ for some $x \in [N]$, and zero otherwise. For some $a_n \in {\mathbb C}$ with $|a_n| \leqslant 1$, we then have $\phi(n) = a_n \mu(n)$; this `throws away' smoothness. With ${\gamma} = 3.1$, the calculation in \cite[\S 6]{densesquares} yields
\begin{equation} \label{CubicBourgain0}
{\delta}^{2{\gamma}} N^{\gamma} R^2 \ll \sum_{r,r' \leqslant R} | \hat \mu({\theta}_r - {\theta}'_r)| ^{\gamma}.
\end{equation}

Consider the value of ${\theta} = {\theta}_r - {\theta}'_r$ in the right-hand side of \eqref{CubicBourgain0}. Define a set of `minor arcs'
\[
{\mathfrak n} = \{ {\alpha} \in {\mathbb T}: |\hat \mu({\alpha})| \leqslant N^{10^{-8}+3/4} \}.
\]
In light of \eqref{wmaBounded}, the contribution from ${\theta} \in {\mathfrak n}$ to the right-hand side of \eqref{CubicBourgain0} is $o({\delta}^{2{\gamma}} N^{\gamma} R^2)$, and so
\begin{equation} \label{CubicBourgain01}
{\delta}^{2{\gamma}} N^{\gamma} R^2 \ll \sum_{\substack{r,r' \leqslant R:\\ {\theta} \notin {\mathfrak n}}} | \hat \mu({\theta}_r - {\theta}'_r)| ^{\gamma}.
\end{equation}

Next, suppose ${\theta} \in {\mathbb T} \setminus {\mathfrak n}$, and fix a small $\varepsilon > 0$. By \cite[Lemma 2.3]{wps}, there exist relatively prime $q \in {\mathbb N}$ and $a \in {\mathbb Z}$ such that 
\[
q \leqslant N^{3/4}, \qquad |q {\theta} - a| \leqslant N^{-9/4}
\]
and
\[
\hat \mu ({\theta}) \ll q^{\varepsilon-\frac13} N (1 + N^3 |{\theta}- a/q|)^{-1/3}.
\]
With $C$ a large positive constant, put $Q= C+{\delta}^{-9}$. The contribution to the right-hand side of \eqref{CubicBourgain01} from denominators $q > Q$ is $O(R^2 N^{\gamma} Q^{{\gamma}(\varepsilon - \frac13)})$, which is negligible compared to the left-hand side. 

Hence
\begin{equation} \label{CubicBourgain02}
{\delta}^{2{\gamma}} R^2 \ll \sum_{1 \leqslant r, r' \leqslant R} G({\theta}_r - {\theta}'_r),
\end{equation}
where
\[
G({\theta}) = \sum_{q \leqslant Q} \sum_{a=0}^{q-1} \frac{q ^{{\gamma}(\varepsilon - \frac 13)}}{ (1+ N^3 | \sin ({\theta} - a/q) |)^{{\gamma}/3}}.
\]
The inequality \eqref{CubicBourgain02} is a cubic version of \cite[Eq. (4.16)]{Bou1989}. As ${\gamma}(\varepsilon - \frac13) > 1$, Bourgain's argument carries through, and yields \eqref{STPcubicBounded}.

label: trivial count
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{trivial count}
Let $k \geqslant 2$, and let $c_1, \ldots, c_s$ be non-zero integers summing to zero. Then there exists $s_0(k)$ such that if $s \geqslant s_0(k)$ then
\[
\# \Bigl\{ {\mathbf x} \in S(N;N^\eta)^s : \sum_{i= 1}^s c_i x_i^k = 0 \text{ and } x_i = x_j \text{ for some } i \neq j \Bigr\} = o\left(  N^{s-k} \right).
\]
Moreover, one can take $s_0(2)=5$, $s_0(3) = 8$, and $s_0(k)$ satisfying \eqref{s0 size}.
head: environment

label: little oh plus one
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $s_0(k)$ be as in Lemma \ref{BabyRestriction}.  By the union bound, it suffices to prove an estimate of the required shape for the number of solutions with $x_{s-1} = x_s$.  In this case we are estimating
$$
\# \Bigl\{ x \in S(N;N^\eta)^{s-1} : \sum_{i = 1}^{s-2} c_i x_i^k + (c_{s-1} + c_s) x_{s-1}^k = 0 \Bigr\}.
$$
It may be that $c_{s-1} + c_s = 0$, so we estimate the contribution from the $x_{s-1}$ variable trivially.  Using orthogonality and H\"older's inequality, it therefore suffices to prove that
\begin{equation}\label{little oh plus one}
\int_\mathbb{T}\Bigl|  \sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta)} e(\alpha x^k) \Bigr|^{s-2} \mathrm{d} \alpha = o(N^{s-1 - k}).
\end{equation}

Let $p = s_0(k) - 10^{-8}$.  When $s-2 \geqslant p$, the estimate \eqref{little oh plus one} follows from Lemma \ref{BabyRestriction} and the trivial estimate $\Bigl|  \sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta)} e(\alpha x^k) \Bigr| \leqslant N$. When $s-2 < p$, we apply H\"older's inequality and Lemma \ref{BabyRestriction} to obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_\mathbb{T}\Bigl|  \sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta)} e(\alpha x^k)  \Bigr|^{s-2} \mathrm{d} \alpha &\leqslant \left( \int_\mathbb{T}\Bigl|  \sum_{x \in S(N;N^\eta) } e(\alpha x^k) \Bigr|^{p} \mathrm{d} \alpha \right)^{\frac{s-2}{p}} 
\\&  \ll  N^{s-2 - \frac{k(s-2)}{p}}.
\end{align*}
It remains to check that 
$
s-2 - \frac{k(s-2)}{p} < s- 1 - k,
$
or equivalently that
$
2 + p(1-\tfrac{1}{k}) < s.
$
Since $s > p$, this follows if $p/k \geqslant 2$, which we can certainly ensure without affecting the bound \eqref{s0 size}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $p = s - \delta$.  By Lemma \ref{restriction additivity}, the weight
$$
\frac{\nu_i}{\left\| \nu_i\right\|_1} + \frac{\mu_i}{\left\| \mu_i\right\|_1}
$$
satisfies a $p$-restriction estimate with constant $K$ and majorises the difference 
$$
\frac{f_i}{\left\| \nu_i\right\|_1} - \frac{g_i}{\left\| \mu_i\right\|_1}.
$$
Observing that this weight has $L^1$ norm equal to two, the lemma follows on applying the telescoping identity 
$$
a_1\dotsm a_s - b_1\dotsm b_s = \sum_{i=1}^s (a_i - b_i)\prod_{j < i} a_j \prod_{j > i} b_j,
$$ 
together with Lemma \ref{gen von neu on a summand}.

label: major
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{major} Suppose $q \in {\mathbb N}$ and $a \in {\mathbb Z}$, with $q \leqslant R/W$ and $\| q {\alpha} \| =  |q {\alpha} - a|$. Then
\[
 \hat \nu ({\alpha}) = \rho(1/\eta) q^{-1} S_{q,a} I \Bigl({\alpha} - \frac a q \Bigr) + O_\eta \Bigl(\frac{P^k}{\log P}(q+ P^k \| q {\alpha} \|) \Bigr).
\]
head: environment
name: First level

title: Proof
body_md:
The start of the proof of \cite[Lemma 5.4]{Vau1989} yields
\[
\sum_{\substack{x \in S(m; R) \\ x \equiv Wr + \xi {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,W}q}} 1 = \frac1{Wq} \sum_{x \in S(m;R)}1 + O\Bigl( \frac{P}{\log P} \Bigr),
\]
valid for $r \in [q]$ and $m \leqslant P$. Therefore 
\[
\sum_{\substack{x \in S(m; R) \\ x \equiv \xi {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,W}}} e \Bigl( \frac a q \cdot \frac{ x^k - \xi^k }{kW} \Bigr) 
= \frac {S_{q,a}}{Wq} \sum_{x \in S(m;R)}1 + O\Bigl( \frac{qP}{\log P} \Bigr).
\]
In particular, if ${\alpha}(x)$ equals $e \Bigl( \frac a q \cdot \frac{ x^k - \xi^k }{kW} \Bigr)$ when $x \equiv \xi {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,W}$ is $R$-smooth and 0 otherwise, then
\[
\sum_{x \leqslant m} \Bigl({\alpha}(x)- \frac{S_{q,a}}{Wq} \rho \Bigl(\frac {\log m}{\log R} \Bigr) \Bigr) \ll \frac{qP}{\log P}.
\]
By partial summation and the boundedness of $\rho'$, we also have
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{x \leqslant m} \rho \Bigl( \frac{ \log x}{\log R} \Bigr) = m \rho \Bigl( \frac{ \log m}{\log R} \Bigr) + O\Bigl( \frac P{\log P} \Bigr) \qquad (1 \leqslant m \leqslant P),
\end{equation*}
and so
\[
\sum_{x \leqslant m} \Bigl( {\alpha}(x) - \frac{S_{q,a}}{Wq}  \rho \Bigl(\frac {\log x}{\log R} \Bigr) \Bigr)  \ll \frac{qP}{\log P}.
\]

Next, observe that with ${\beta} = {\alpha} - a/q$ we have $|{\beta}| = q^{-1} \|q {\alpha} \|$ and
\begin{align}
 \notag \hat \nu ({\alpha}) &= 
\sum_{\substack{x \in S(P;R) \\ x \equiv \xi {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,W}}} e \Bigl( \frac a q \cdot \frac{ x^k - \xi^k }{kW} \Bigr) \phi(x) \\
\label{VaughanWay} &= \frac{ S_{q,a}}{Wq}  \sum_{x \leqslant P} \rho \Bigl( \frac{ \log x}{ \log R} \Bigr) \phi(x) + E,
\end{align}
where 
\[
\phi(x) = x^{k-1} e \Bigl( {\beta} \frac{ x^k - \xi^k }{kW} \Bigr)
\]
and
\[
E = \sum_{x \leqslant P} \Bigl({\alpha}(x)- \frac{S_{q,a}}{Wq} \rho \Bigl(\frac {\log x}{\log R} \Bigr) \Bigr) \phi(x).
\]
Partial summation gives
\[
E \ll  \frac{qP}{\log P} ( \| \phi \|_{L^\infty ([1,P])} + P \| \phi'\|_{L^\infty ([1,P])} ) \ll \frac{qP^k}{\log P} (1+ P^k | {\beta} |),
\]
and with the boundedness of $\rho'$ it also implies that
\[
\sum_{x \leqslant P} \rho \Bigl( \frac{ \log x}{ \log R} \Bigr) \phi(x) = 
\rho(1/\eta) \sum_{x \leqslant P} \phi(x) + O \Bigl( \frac{ P^k}{\log P} \Bigr).
\]
Meanwhile, Euler--Maclaurin summation \cite[Eq. (4.8)]{vaughan97} yields
\begin{align*}
\sum_{x \leqslant P} \phi(x) &= \int_1^P \phi(x) {\mathrm{d}} x + O(P^{k-1} (1+ P^k | {\beta} |)) 
\\&= WI({\beta}) + O(P^{k-1} (1+ P^k | {\beta} |)).
\end{align*}
Substituting these estimates into \eqref{VaughanWay} concludes the proof.

title: Lemma

label: decompose
title: Proof
body_md:
Plainly $S_{1,0} = 1$, so let $q \geqslant 2$, and let $a \in {\mathbb Z}$ with $(q,a) = 1$. The binomial expansion gives
\[
S_{q,a} =\sum_{r {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,q}} e_q\Biggl(a \sum_{\ell = 1}^k \frac{{k \choose \ell} W^{\ell - 1}}k \xi^{k-\ell} r^\ell \Biggr),
\]
and we note that $\frac{{k \choose \ell} W^{\ell - 1}}k \in {\mathbb Z}$ ($1 \leqslant \ell \leqslant k$). Write $q = uv$, where $u$ is $w$-smooth and $(v,W) = 1$. Since $(u,v) = 1$, a standard calculation reveals that
\begin{equation} \label{decompose}
S_{q,a} = S_{u,a_1} S_{v,a_2},
\end{equation}
where $a_1 = av^{-1} \in ({\mathbb Z} / u {\mathbb Z})^\times$ and $a_2 = au^{-1} \in ({\mathbb Z} / v {\mathbb Z})^\times$ (see \cite[Lemma 2.10]{vaughan97}). 

Put $u = hu'$, where $h = (u, W/k)$. Representing $r{\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,q}$ as $r = r_1 + u' r_2$, where $0 \leqslant r_1 < u'$ and $0 \leqslant r_2 < h$, gives
\begin{align*}
S(u,a_1) &= \sum_{\substack{0 \leqslant r_1 < u' \\ 0 \leqslant r_2 < h}}  e_{hu'} \Biggl(a_1 \sum_{\ell = 1}^k {k \choose \ell} \frac{{k \choose \ell} W^{\ell - 1}}k \xi^{k-\ell} (r_1 + u'r_2)^\ell \Biggr) \\
&= 
\sum_{r_1 = 0}^{u'-1}   e_{hu'} \Biggl(a_1 \sum_{\ell = 1}^k \frac{{k \choose \ell} W^{\ell - 1}}k \xi^{k-\ell} r_1^\ell \Biggr)\\
& \qquad  \cdot \sum_{r_2 = 0 }^{h-1} e_h 
\Biggl(a_1 \sum_{\ell = 1}^k \frac{{k \choose \ell} W^{\ell - 1}}k \xi^{k-\ell} (u')^{\ell - 1} r_2^\ell \Biggr).
\end{align*}
As $h$ divides $W/k$, the inner sum is
\[
\sum_{r_2 {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,h}} e_h (a_1 \xi^{k-1} r_2),
\]
which vanishes unless $h \mid a_1 \xi^{k-1}$. As $(h,a_1) = (h,\xi) = 1$, and as
\[
(u,W/k) = 1 \Leftrightarrow (u,W) = 1 \Leftrightarrow u =1,
\]
we conclude that
\begin{equation} \label{vanishing}
S_{u,a_1} = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } u \ne 1 \\
1 &\text{if } u =1.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Moreover, note that if $2 \leqslant q \leqslant w$ then $u =q$ and $v = 1$. Now \eqref{decompose} and \eqref{vanishing} complete the proof of \eqref{complete1}. 

Next we prove \eqref{complete2}. By \eqref{decompose} and \eqref{vanishing}, we may assume $u =1$. Consider
\[
e_{kWv}(a_2 \xi^k) S_{v,a_2} = \sum_{r {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,v}} e_v \Bigl(a_2 \frac{(Wr + \xi)^k}{kW} \Bigr).
\]
As $(v,W) = 1$, we can change variables by $t = \xi W^{-1} + r \in {\mathbb Z} / v {\mathbb Z}$, which gives
\[
e_{kWv}(a_2 \xi^k) S_{v,a_2} = \sum_{t {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,v}} e_v \Bigl(a_2 \frac{W^{k-1}}k t^k\Bigr).
\]
Since $\Bigl( v, a_2 \frac{W^{k-1}}k \Bigr) = 1$, we may apply \cite[Theorem 4.2]{vaughan97}, which gives
\[
S_{v,a_2} \ll v^{1-1/k} = q^{1-1/k}.
\]
By \eqref{decompose} and \eqref{vanishing}, we now have $S_{q,a} \ll q^{1-1/k}$.

label: minor0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{minor0} Suppose $0 < {\delta} < (2k)^{-1}$, and let ${\mathfrak m}_1$ denote the set of real numbers ${\gamma}$ with the property that if $a \in {\mathbb Z}$, $q \in {\mathbb N}$, $(a,q)=1$ and $|q {\gamma} - a| \leqslant P^{\frac12-k + {\delta} k}$ then $q > P^{\frac12 + {\delta} k}$. Put
\[
\iota(k) = \max_{{\lambda} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\geqslant 2}} \frac1{4{\lambda}} (1- (k-2) (1-1/k)^{{\lambda}-2}).
\]
Then, assuming $\eta \leqslant \eta_0(\varepsilon,k)$, we have
\[
\hat \nu({\alpha}) \ll P^{k + \varepsilon} (P^{- {\delta}}+P^{ -\iota(k)}) \qquad ({\alpha} \in kW {\mathfrak m}_1).
\]
head: environment
name: Minor arcs

title: Remark
body_md: We will later apply this with $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_k$, so that the condition $\eta \leqslant \eta_0(\varepsilon,k)$ will be met.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Following the proof of \cite[Theorem 1.8]{Vau1989}, we find that if ${\alpha} \in {\mathfrak m}_1$ and $1 \leqslant m \leqslant P$ then
\[
\sum_{x \in S(m;R)} e \Bigl(\frac {\alpha} {kW} x^k + \frac tW x \Bigr) \ll P^{1+\varepsilon} (P^{- {\delta}}+P^{ -\iota(k)}).
\]
Indeed, already built into that proof are bounds uniform over linear twists; see \cite[Eq. (10.9)]{Vau1989}. The sum above is over $x \in S(m;R)$, where $1 \leqslant m \leqslant P$, rather than over $x \in S(P;R)$, however we can assume that $\sqrt P \leqslant m \leqslant P$ and then run Vaughan's argument.

Now, by \eqref{StartingPoint}, we have
\[
\sum_{\substack{x \in S(m;R) \\ x \equiv \xi {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,W}}} e \Bigl( {\alpha} \frac{x^k - \xi^k}{kW} \Bigr)
\ll P^{1+\varepsilon} (P^{- {\delta}}+P^{ -\iota(k)}).
\]
From here, partial summation gives
\[
\hat \nu({\alpha}) = \sum_{\substack{x \in S(P;R) \\ x \equiv \xi {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,W}}} x^{k-1} e \Bigl( {\alpha} \frac{x^k - \xi^k}{kW} \Bigr)
\ll P^{k+\varepsilon} (P^{- {\delta}}+P^{ -\iota(k)}).
\]
head: environment

label: prune1
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: First pruning step

title: Proof
body_md:
By partial summation and \eqref{StartingPoint}, it suffices to show that if $\sqrt{P} \leqslant m \leqslant P$ then
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{x \in S(m;R)} e \Bigl(\frac {\alpha} {kW} x^k + \frac tW x \Bigr) \\
&\quad \ll P(\log P)^3 q^\varepsilon ( (q + P^k|q {\alpha} - a|)^{-1/(2k)}
+ (MR/P)^{1/2} + q^{\frac12 - \frac1{2k}}  (R/M)^{1/2}).
\end{align*}
To show this, we work through the proof of \cite[Lemma 7.2]{VW1991}; the inner sum of Eq. (7.4) therein becomes
\[
S = \sum_{y \in I \cap {\mathbb Z}} e \Bigl( \frac {\alpha} {kW} p^k (u_2^k - u_1^k)y^k + \frac tW p (u_2 - u_1)y \Bigr),
\]
where 
\[
I = (V/p, \min \{2V/p, m/(u_1p), m/(u_2p) \} ]
\]
is an interval of length at most $V/p$ and $u_1,u_2,p$ are the outer summation variables in \cite[Eq. (7.4)]{VW1991}. With reference to that proof, we have
\[
D = \gcd(kWq, ap^k(u_2^k-u_1^k), t qk p (u_2 - u_1)) \ll_{k,W} (q, p^k(u_2^k-u_1^k)),
\]
and
\[
S = \sum_{y \in I \cap {\mathbb Z}} e_{q'}(a' y^k + b' y) e({\beta} y^k),
\]
where 
\[
Dq' = kWq, \quad  Da' = ap^k(u_1^k - u_2^k),\quad  Db' = tkqp (u_2 - u_1),
\]
$\gcd(a',b',q') = 1$ and
\[ 
{\beta} = \frac{ p^k(u_2^k - u_1^k) } {kW} ({\alpha} - a/q).
\]

Continuing to follow the proof of \cite[Lemma 7.2]{VW1991}, we now apply \cite[Lemma 4.4]{Bak1986} and \cite[Theorems 7.1 and 7.3]{vaughan97} in lieu of the more specific \cite[Lemma 2.8 and Theorems 4.1 and 4.2]{vaughan97}. One can check that
\[
|q {\beta}| \leqslant (2k^2)^{-1} (V/p)^{1-k}.
\]
As $|I| \leqslant V/p$, this condition enables us to apply \cite[Lemma 4.4]{Bak1986}, giving
\[
S = (q')^{-1}\sum_{x \leqslant q'} e_{q'}(a' x^k + b' x) \int_I e({\beta} z^k) {\mathrm{d}} z + O(q^{1- \frac1k+\varepsilon} ).
\]
The error term $RU^2 q^{\frac12+\varepsilon}$ in \cite[Eq. (7.5)]{VW1991} is enlarged to $RU^2 q^{1- \frac1k+  \varepsilon }$, and the effect of applying \cite[Theorems 7.1 and 7.3]{vaughan97} is to increase the quantity $S_3$ appearing therein by a multiplicative factor of $O_{\varepsilon,k,W}(q^{\varepsilon/8})$. 

The remainder of the proof of \cite[Lemma 7.2]{VW1991} carries through in the present context, \emph{mutatis mutandis}. The eventual outcome of the changes above is to increase the term $q^{1/4} P (R/M)^{1/2}$ to $q^{\frac12 - \frac1{2k}} P (R/M)^{1/2}$, and we obtain the asserted bound.
head: environment

label: prune2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{prune2} Suppose $R = P^\eta$ with $0 < \eta < 1/2$, and that $a,q \in {\mathbb Z}$ with $(a,q) = 1$ and $1 \leqslant q \leqslant (\log P)^A$. Then for some $c = c(\eta,A)$ we have
\[
\hat \nu({\alpha}) \ll_{\varepsilon,k,w,\eta,A,c} P^k (q + P^k|q {\alpha} - a|)^{\varepsilon- \frac1k}
+ P^k \cdot \exp( - c \sqrt{\log P}) (1 + P^k |{\alpha} - a/q|).
\]
head: environment
name: Second pruning step

title: Proof
body_md:
Again we apply partial summation and \eqref{StartingPoint}, leaving us to show that if $P^{0.99} \leqslant m \leqslant P$ then
\begin{align*}
g({\alpha}) &:= \sum_{x \in S(m;R)} e \Bigl(\frac {\alpha} {kW} x^k + \frac tW x \Bigr)  \\
&\ll  P (q + P^k|q {\alpha} - a|)^{\varepsilon- \frac1k} + P \cdot \exp( - c \sqrt {\log P}) (1 + P^k |{\alpha} - a/q|).
\end{align*}
This time we follow the proof of \cite[Lemma 8.5]{VW1991}. Writing ${\beta} = {\alpha} - a/q$, this  initially formats our smooth Weyl sum as
\begin{align*}
g({\alpha}) = \sum_{\substack{d \mid kWq \\ q/d \in S(m;R)}} \sum_{\substack{y =1 \\ (y,d)=1}}^d 
&e((kWq/d)^{k-1} y^k a/d + tkqy/d)  \\ &\quad \cdot \Psi \Bigl( \frac{md}{kWq} , R; d, y, \frac{{\beta}(kWq/d)^k }{kW} \Bigr),
\end{align*}
where
\[
\Psi(Q,R; d,y, {\gamma}) = \sum_{\substack{z \in S(Q; R) \\ z \equiv y {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,d}}} e( {\gamma} z^k).
\]
The calculation by Vaughan and Wooley in the proof of \cite[Lemma 8.5]{VW1991} ensures that $\Psi(Q,R;d,y,{\gamma})$ is, up to a small additive error, independent of $y$. As $m \leqslant P$ and $kW \ll_{k,W}1$, the outcome of this calculation is unaffected, and we obtain
\begin{align*}
g({\alpha}) &\ll P(1+P^k |{\beta}|)^{-1/k} \\&\qquad \cdot
\Bigl(\exp(- c \sqrt{\log P}) + \sum_{d \mid kWq} \frac{d}{q \varphi(d)} |{\mathcal W}(d, a(kWq/d)^{k-1}, tkq)| \Bigr),
\end{align*}
where
\[
{\mathcal W}(Q,A,B) = \sum_{\substack{y {\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\,Q} \\ (y,Q)=1}} e_Q(Ay^k + By).
\]
Our final task is to show that if $d \mid kWq$ then
\begin{equation*}
{\mathcal W}(d, a(kWq/d)^{k-1}, tkq) \ll_{k,w, \varepsilon} q^{1-\frac1k + \varepsilon}.
\end{equation*}

One may readily verify the usual multiplicativity property: if $(Q_1, Q_2) = 1$ then
\begin{equation} \label{FirstHua}
{\mathcal W}(Q_1 Q_2, A, B) = {\mathcal W}(Q_1, AQ_2^{k-1}, B) \cdot {\mathcal W}(Q_2, AQ_1^{k-1}, B);
\end{equation}
see \cite[Lemma 8.1]{Hua}. Next we analyse 
\[
{\mathcal W} (p^i, A, tkq),
\]
when $p$ is prime and $p^i \| d$. If $p > w$ then $p^i \mid tkq$, so 
\[
{\mathcal W}(p^i, A, tkq) = {\mathcal W}(p^i, A, 0) \ll p^{i/2} (p^i, A)^{1/2},
\]
using \cite[Lemma 8.4]{VW1991}. Meanwhile, if $p \leqslant w$ then we use the identity
\[
{\mathcal W}(p^i, A, tkq) = S(p^i, A, tkq) - S( p^{i-1}, Ap^{k-1}, tkq),
\]
where
\[
S(Q, A, B) = \sum_{y \leqslant Q} e_Q( Ay^k + By).
\]
Since $p \leqslant w$, we have 
\[
\gcd(p^i,A, tkq) , \: \gcd(p^{i-1}, Ap^{k-1}, tkq) \ll_{k,w} (p^i,A),
\]
so we may use \cite[Eq. (7.9)]{vaughan97} to infer that
\[
{\mathcal W}(p^i, A, tkq) \ll_{k,w} (p^i,A)^{1/k} (p^i)^{1- \frac1k}.
\]
In both cases we have
\[
|{\mathcal W}(p^i, A, tkq)| \leqslant c_{k,w} (p^i,A)^{1/k} (p^i)^{1- \frac1k},
\]
and inputting this into \eqref{FirstHua} reveals that
\[
{\mathcal W}(d, A, tkq) \ll q^\varepsilon (d,A)^{1/k} d^{1-\frac1k}.
\]

Apply this with $A = a (kWq/d)^{k-1}$. With this choice of $A$, we have
\begin{align*}
(d,A) \leqslant (d,a) (d,(kWq/d)^{k-1}) &\leqslant (kWq,a)  (d,(kWq/d)^{k-1})
\\ &\leqslant kW (d,(kWq/d)^{k-1}).
\end{align*}
Letting $p^i \| d$ and $p^j \| kWq$ gives
\[
(d,A) \ll_{k,w} \prod_p p^{\min \{i, (k-1)(j-i)\} },
\]
and so
\begin{align*}
{\mathcal W}(d, a(kWq/d)^{k-1}, tkq) &\ll q^\varepsilon \prod_{\substack{p^i \| d \\ p^j \| kWq}} p^{i(1-\frac1k) + k^{-1} \min \{i, (k-1)(j-i)\}}
\\ &\ll q^\varepsilon \prod_{p^j \| kWq} (p^j)^{1-\frac1k} \ll q^{1-\frac1k+\varepsilon}.
\end{align*}

title: Proof

\[

where ${\mathcal N}$ is the number of solutions $({\mathbf x}, {\mathbf{y}}) \in S(P;P^\eta)^m \times S(P;P^\eta)^m$ to the Diophantine equation
\[

title: Proof
body_md:
Rogovskaya \cite{Rogovskaya} showed that the system
\begin{align*}
x_1 + x_2 + x_3 &= y_1 + y_2 + y_3 \\
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 &= y_1^2 + y_2^2 + y_3^2
\end{align*}
has $\frac{18}{\pi^2} P^3 \log P + O(P^3)$ solutions $({\mathbf x}, {\mathbf{y}}) \in [P]^6$. By orthogonality, one can deduce from this that
\[
\int_{{\mathbb T}^2} \Bigl| \sum_{|x| \leqslant P} e({\alpha}_1 x + {\alpha}_2 x^2) \Bigr|^6 {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha}_1 {\mathrm{d}} {\alpha}_2 \ll P^3 \log P.
\]
As $t \geqslant 6$, the lemma now follows from orthogonality, H\"older's inequality, and the trivial bound $\sum_{|x| \leqslant P} e({\alpha}_1 x + {\alpha}_2 x^2) \ll P$.
head: environment

label: N1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{N1}
We have
\[
{\mathcal N}_1 \gg P^{t-2}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\begin{align*}
Q(y_1,\ldots,y_{t-1}) &= c_t^{-1} (c_1y_1 + \cdots + c_{t-1} y_{t-1})^2 + \sum_{i \leqslant t-1} c_iy_i^2 \\
&= \sum_{i \leqslant t-1} (c_i + c_i^2/c_t)y_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \leqslant i < j \leqslant t-1} (c_i c_j/c_t) y_i y_j,
\end{align*}
and put
\[
C = |c_1| + \cdots + |c_t|.
\]
Now ${\mathcal N}_1$ is greater than or equal to the number of integer solutions
\[
(y,y_1,\ldots,y_{t-1}) \in [-P/C,P/C]^t
\]
to
\[
ay^2 + Q(y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}) = 0
\]
with $c_1 y_1 + \cdots + c_{t-1} y_{t-1} \equiv 0 \mod c_t$. By considering only multiples of $c_t$, we find that ${\mathcal N}_1$ is greater than or equal to the number of integer solutions ${\mathbf x} \in [-P/C^2,P/C^2]^t$ to
\[
Q_1({\mathbf x}) := Q(x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1}) +ax_t^2 = 0.
\]

For the sake of brevity, we appeal to Birch's very general theorem \cite[Theorem 1]{Birch}. The \emph{Birch singular locus} is the set ${\mathcal S}$ of ${\mathbf x} \in {\mathbb C}^t$ at which the gradient of $Q_1$ vanishes identically. (In this instance, the Birch singular locus coincides with the usual singular locus.) We compute that
\[
\frac12 \partial_i Q(y_1,\ldots, y_{t-1}) = (c_i + c_i^2/c_t) y_i + \sum_{\substack{j \leqslant t- 1 \\ j \ne i}} c_i c_j y_j / c_t,
\]
and so
\[
\frac{c_t}{2c_i} \partial_i Q = (c_t + c_i) y_i + \sum_{\substack{j \leqslant t- 1 \\ j \ne i}} c_j y_j = c_t ( y_i - y_t) + \sum_{j \leqslant t} c_j y_j = c_t ( y_i - y_t),
\]
where $y_t := -c_t^{-1} (c_1y_1 + \cdots + c_{t-1}y_{t-1})$. Therefore
\[
{\mathcal S} = \{ (x,x,\ldots,x,0) \in {\mathbb C}^t \},
\]
and in particular $\dim {\mathcal S} = 1$. 

As $t - \dim {\mathcal S} > 4$, Birch's theorem \cite[Theorem 1]{Birch} gives
\begin{equation} \label{BirchAsymptotic}
{\mathcal N}_1 = {\mathfrak S} {\mathfrak J} P^{t-2} + O(P^{t-2-{\delta}}),
\end{equation}
for some constant ${\delta} > 0$, where ${\mathfrak S}$ and ${\mathfrak J}$ are respectively the \emph{singular series} and \emph{singular integral} arising from the circle method analysis. Birch notes in \cite[\S 7]{Birch} that ${\mathfrak S}$ is positive as long as $Q_1$ has a non-singular $p$-adic zero for each prime $p$, and that ${\mathfrak J}$ is positive as long as $Q_1$ has a real zero outside of ${\mathcal S}_1$. Note that $Q$ has a zero ${\mathbf x}^* \in {\mathbb Z}^{t-1}$ with pairwise distinct coordinates; this follows from \cite[Theorem 1.1]{Keil}, or from a circle method analysis. Now $({\mathbf x}^*,0)$ is a real zero of $Q_1$ outside of ${\mathcal S}_1$, and is also a non-singular $p$-adic zero for each $p$. Hence ${\mathfrak S} {\mathfrak J} > 0$, and by \eqref{BirchAsymptotic} the proof is now complete.
